region.en: Benin-Oyo border country (symbolic pin: the east, whence the sun comes)
region.zh: 貝寧與奧約交界地帶（象徵定位：日出之東方）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XIX

summary.en: While Osa'lubwa, the maker, was fashioning man he left the work unfinished; Esu came along and finished the figure according to his own ideas. When Osa'lubwa returned and saw what had been done he was much annoyed, and banished Esu to the east, whence the sun comes.
summary.zh: 造物者奧薩盧布瓦塑人之時，工程半輟；艾舒路過，按自己的心意把人補完。奧薩盧布瓦歸來見狀大怒，將艾舒放逐到日出之東方。

sensitivity.note: Recorded by Dennett among the Bini (Benin) as a shared Yoruba-Bini mythic stratum; Esu (Èṣù) is the Yoruba trickster deity. The 'unfinished and finished by another' motif is a strong cross-tradition parallel to trickster-spoiling-creation tales. Recorded 1906 in colonial-era ethnography.

title.en: The Old Lady Banished to the Moon

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the moon seen from the Ogun country)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：奧貢之鄉仰望的月亮）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XIX

summary.en: On the first day of the week — the day of rest — an old woman would insist on cutting wood, though the axe is taboo on Ogun's day; she was banished to the moon, where her figure may still be traced. Ogun himself is the blacksmith who, by the help of fire, makes his implements.
summary.zh: 週首之日（安息之日）本不得動斧，一位老婦偏偏執意劈柴，違犯奧貢日之禁；她被放逐到月亮上去，月面上的身影至今猶見。奧貢正是那位借火之力鍛造工具的鐵匠之神。

sensitivity.note: Moon-banishment etiology tied to Ogun's rest-day taboo; recorded 1906 by Dennett in the Bini-Yoruba border country. Cross-tradition parallels (mark on the moon) are widespread; presented as archival record.

title.en: The Chief Who Built a Ladder to the Home of Thunder

region.en: Sapoba road, Benin (symbolic pin: the tree marking where the ladder fell)
region.zh: 奈及利亞貝寧薩波巴道（象徵定位：梯斷之處的紀念樹）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XIX

summary.en: The great war chief Ezomo heard it thunder and, taking the storm for an enemy of the Oba who wished to fight him, built a ladder to reach the home of thunder. When he and all his people were on the ladder and just getting at the home of thunder, it gave way, and the top of it fell where a tree now grows — planted, with mound and cowries, to mark the place.
summary.zh: 大戰酋長埃佐莫聞雷聲大作，誤以為是奧巴王的仇敵前來挑戰，遂造長梯直上雷電之宮。正當他率領全部人馬登梯、將抵雷宮之際，長梯折斷，梯頂墜落之處如今長著一棵大樹——土丘貝幣環繞，正是紀念之地。

sensitivity.note: Bini legend about war with the thunder-power (read here as the Yoruba thunder-complex of Shango); the heaven-storming ladder is a world motif (cf. Tower of Babel). Recorded 1906.

passages.text: On the Sapoba road there is a tree with the usual mound of earth and cowries in front of it, planted they say to mark the place where the top of Ezomo's ladder fell. The story goes that this great war chief heard it thunder and wanted to know what enemy of the Oba's it was who evidently wished to fight him, so he built a ladder to reach up to the heavens. When he and all his people were on the ladder and just getting at the home of thunder, it gave way, and the top end of it fell where the tree is growing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XIX (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Ovia, the Slandered Wife, Becomes a River
title.zh: 奧維亞——受誣的王妃化為河

region.en: Ovia river, Benin (the river named for the runaway wife)
region.zh: 奈及利亞奧維亞河（以出走王妃為名的河流）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XXI

summary.en: Ovia is said to have been one of the wives of Awlawyo, the Alafin of Oyo. A jealous rival slipped a rat and water into her cloth and told the Alafin that Ovia had fouled herself; in his anger he shamed her, and she cried and ran away. When the truth came out he killed the slanderer and begged Ovia to return, but she refused — nor would she come back when Okwo was sent to fetch her, fearing to return without her, and the two became river spirits in the Benin country, Ovia's sign being the dress of strips of palm leaves.
summary.zh: 相傳奧維亞曾是奧約阿勞芬王（奧拉沃約）的妃子。嫉妒者把老鼠和水塞進她的衣袍，向王告發她「失禁污衣」；王大怒羞辱於她，她泣而出走。真相大白後，王誅殺讒婦，求她回宮，她不肯；遣奧科沃前去接她，亦遭拒絕——奧科沃不敢空手而回，二人遂在貝寧之地化作河靈。奧維亞的聖徵是棕櫚葉編織之裙。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1906 among the Bini, but explicitly names the Alafin of Oyo — a Yoruba-Bini shared legend. Ovia remains one of the great living cults of Benin. Cross-ref with the Shango-Oya flight cycle.

passages.text: Ovia is said to have been one of the wives of Awlawyo, the Alafin of Awyaw (Oyo). A wife who was jealous of her put a rat and some water into her cloth, and then went and told the Alafin that Ovia had made water in her cloth. Awlawyo was very cross with her, so she cried and ran away. And when Awlawyo made inquiries, and found out that he had been deceived, he killed the jealous wife, and asked Ovia to come back to him, but she refused. Then he sent Okwo to bring her back, but she refused to go back, and Okwo feared to return without her; so they both became river spirits in the Benin country. The sign of the Ovia is the dress made of strips of palm leaves.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XXI (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Olukun and Oha: The Hiccough That Broke a Marriage
title.zh: 奧魯貢與奧哈——一聲打嗝拆散的水族婚

region.en: Benin river country (symbolic pin: the great Benin river of Olukun)
region.zh: 貝寧水鄉（象徵定位：奧魯貢大河）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XXI

summary.en: Oha drank Ainyo and hiccoughed, which so vexed her husband Olukun that she ran away from him. Olukun wept — for in those days he was very poor. Then Olukun married Igbagon and grew rich; and when Oha wished to return and prayed his forgiveness, he, being rich now, forgave her — but only on condition that she come back as the wood-bearer to Igbagon.
summary.zh: 奧哈飲了阿伊尼約之水，打了個嗝，竟觸怒丈夫奧魯貢，她遂負氣出走。彼時奧魯貢尚且貧窮，唯有哭泣。後來他娶了伊格巴貢，日漸富足；奧哈悔悟歸來求恕，已富貴的奧魯貢原諒了她——但只准她回來做伊格巴貢的拾柴婢。

sensitivity.note: River-marriage myth of the Benin Olukun (identifiable with the Yoruba sea-god Olokun), recorded 1906. Names of rivers are marriage-linked in this water-pantheon tale.

passages.text: Oha drank Ainyo and hiccoughed, which vexed Olukun, so she ran away from him. Olukun cried. This was when Olukun was very poor. Then Olukun married Igbagon. Then Oha wished to return and prayed Olukun to forgive her. He was rich now, so he forgave her and said she might come back, but as the wood bearer to Igbagon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XXI (1906); not verbatim.

region.en: Yoruba-Bini animal country (symbolic pin: famine council ground near Benin)
region.zh: 貝寧獸國（象徵定位：饑年聚義場）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XXI

summary.en: In famine the animals agree to eat their mothers one by one, the parrot secretly sparing his own in a hidden hole with a rope. Tortoise the deceiver spies out the hiding-place and betrays it; the elephant's song fails, but Tortoise's song deceives the mother parrot into lowering the rope — until her son returns singing the cut-rope song: let the elephant fall and crush the tortoise.
summary.zh: 饑年獸國盟約：輪流奉獻己母為食。鸚鵡暗藏其母於地穴，穴中藏繩。騙子龜君窺得密窟並告發眾獸；大象以歌誘母，未果；龜君一曲竟騙得母鸚鵡垂下繩索。危急之際，兒子鸚鵡歸來高唱斷繩之歌——「母親啊，砍斷繩子！讓大象摔落，壓碎那龜！」

sensitivity.note: Animal trickster tale of the Tortoise (Ijapa/Igwi) cycle, told Dennett 1906 among the Bini with the Yoruba trickster-tortoise; the tortoise's bad character ('a deceiver') is stated in the source.

passages.text: There is a story that says one day Igwi (the tortoise) was a person, and all animals spoke one language. There was a famine in the land. A meeting was called, and it was decided that all should bring in their mothers. The elephant brought in his mother. They killed and ate her. And each day an animal brought in its mother, and they always gave some of the meat to the parrot, most of which he preserved. And when each animal had killed its mother they told the parrot to go and fetch his; but he had hidden his mother away in a hole where she kept a rope. As he refused to bring in his mother all the animals set about to look for her, but they could not find her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XXI (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Then the Igwi watched the parrot and found the mother's hiding-place, and told all the other animals. When they all knew where the mother parrot was to be found they asked the parrot to go on an errand for them to a distant part, and he went — but returned quickly to the court-house and found no one there, for, guided by the Igwi, they had gone to find his mother. When they were near the hole the elephant sang a song, thinking the mother would take his voice for her son's; but she was not taken in. Then the Igwi sang, and the mother parrot was deceived and put out the rope for him. All the animals seized hold of the rope. But just then the son parrot came along and sang to his mother, telling her to cut the rope: "O Mother, Mother, cut the rope! Let the elephant fall, Mother, and crush the tortoise, Mother!" — and so it was done.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XXI (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Eware and the Two Hundred and One Powers

region.en: Benin City, Nigeria (the temple where the powers were burnt)
region.zh: 奈及利亞貝寧城（神力被焚的廟宇）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XXII

summary.en: Eware, a son of the sixth king of Benin, was refused the throne and driven into the bush; after 201 years he returned with 201 followers who, like men, were not really men but Ebami — powers dwelling in rivers and sacred groves. He taught the people the foundation of their religion; but the people, saying there were too many Ebami, built a fine temple, feasted the powers, fastened the doors, and burned the house down. Many escaped into the rivers and became river spirits.
summary.zh: 貝寧第六王之子埃瓦雷求位不遂，被逐入林。二〇一年後，他攜二〇一隨從歸城——他們形似人而非人，是棲於河川聖林的「埃巴米」神力。埃瓦雷傳授宗教之本；但民眾嫌神力太多，建美廟設宴灌醉，閉門縱火焚屋。倖存者紛紛遁入河川，化為河靈。

sensitivity.note: Founding legend of the Benin religion as told to Dennett by a babalawo (1906); the 201 Ebami parallel the Yoruba reckoning of 401/600 powers and the Bini bronze plates that recorded them in the Oba's palace.

passages.text: Eware, he said, was a son of the sixth king of Benin, and when his father died he wished to succeed to the throne. The people, however, would not have him, and drove him into the bush. After 201 years he returned to Benin city with 201 followers. He and his followers were like men but were not really men; they were Ebami (powers in rivers and sacred groves) — Eware then taught the Bini people the foundation of their present religion. But the people said that there were too many Ebami and set about thinking how their number could be diminished. They built a fine house or temple and invited them all to a feast; then gave them plenty to eat and drink, and when they were nearly drunk fastened the doors and burned the house down. Many of the Ebami escaped and entered the different rivers and became river spirits.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XXII (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: God Comes Down to Talk About Death

region.en: Benin City, Nigeria (symbolic pin: the road by which God walked in via Agbor, Oza and Ugo)
region.zh: 奈及利亞貝寧城（象徵定位：神經阿格博爾、奧扎與烏戈入城之路）

source.work: R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (London, 1906), ch. XXII

summary.en: Eware, returned from exile, was much troubled that he had to die, and sent a messenger to Oyisa (God) asking him to come and talk the matter over. God came down, landed at Agbor east of Benin City, was told that was not the city, and was directed via Oza and Ugo until he arrived and met Eware — when it was finally decided that every man must die. Esu, the devil, is said to have accompanied Oyisa bearing a knife.
summary.zh: 流亡歸來的埃瓦雷煩惱於自己終有一死，遣使請奧伊薩（神）下凡相商。神降於貝寧城東的阿格博爾，被告知此非王城，遂經奧扎、烏戈一路問路而至，與埃瓦雷相見——最終議定：凡人皆須一死。相傳惡神艾舒持刀隨行。

sensitivity.note: Origin-of-death decision myth recorded 1906 (Bini setting, Yoruba names Oyisa/Esu). Strong member of the origin-of-death cluster (messenger of death accords). Cross-refs: san-kaggen-eland (origin of death), hindu-rigveda-yama-yami.

passages.text: Eware also was much troubled about the fact that he had to die, so he sent a messenger to Oyisa (= God) to ask him to come to Benin city and talk the matter over. God came down and landed at Agbor, a place to the east of Benin city, and asked if that were Benin city. They told him no, and directed him via Oza and Ugo to the city, so that at length he arrived and had a meeting with Eware, when it was finally decided that every man must die. Eshu (the devil) is said to have accompanied Oyisa bearing a knife.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind, ch. XXII (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Gods Are Called Orisha: The Quarrelled Potsherd
title.zh: 奧里莎之名的由來——陶片之爭

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the shrine where the potsherd is kept, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費附近供陶片的小祠）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: Two friends, Anini and Ogbek, quarrelled over a potsherd (isha) that had been given as a present and then, out of envy, demanded back; elders interfered, the returned sherd was accounted sacred and worshipped — and from this, it is said, every object of worship was afterwards called an Orisha (Ori-isha). Bishop Johnson records another etymology: Orunmila sent beings out to search for and gather the wisdom he had strewn about, and those who succeeded — 'those who were successful in making their collection' — became objects of worship.
summary.zh: 友人阿尼尼與奧格貝克為一片陶器起爭執：一方贈出，另一方因嫉而索回；長老調停後，這片被退回的陶片竟被尊為聖物受人膜拜——自此一切崇拜之物皆名為「奧里莎」（ ori-isha，即「陶片之頭」）。約翰遜主教另記一說：奧倫米拉曾遣眾靈四出搜集他散落世間的智慧，凡搜集有成者（「得其所得者」）遂成受祭之神。

sensitivity.note: Recorded 1906 from Bishop James Johnson (an African bishop of Yoruba origin) — an insider-adjacent Yoruba source. Etiology of the word orisha.

passages.text: Others have represented the term Orisha as derived from the circumstance of a serious difference on a particular occasion between two friends named Anini and Ogbek, a difference in which some elders interfered, over a potsherd (isha) which the one had made a present of to the other, but a return of which the giver afterwards from envy demanded, and which after its return was accounted sacred and became an object of worship; and they say that from this every other object of worship has been called an Orisha (Ori-isha), in allusion to the potsherd over which there had been a severe difference.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: These deities are generally known among us as Orishas, a term which, after the religious tradition of the country, was originally applied to some beings whom Ifa, or Orunmila, the Son of God, had sent out with others to search about for and collect together the wisdom which he had strewn about, and who were successful in their search and collection whilst others failed, and who were then spoken of as Awon ti o ri sha — those who were successful in making their collection — and who after, and in consequence of this, became objects of worship.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Six Hundred: Two Hundred on the Right, Four Hundred on the Left

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the pantheon at Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費萬神殿）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: The number of Yoruba gods commonly reckoned is 401, but it is strictly more correct, says Bishop Johnson, to say 600, arranged under two divisions: 200, as the babalawos would say, placed on the right-hand side, and 400 on the left-hand side — with Ifa, Oduduwa, Obanta and Obanla, Oshun, Ogun, Yemaja, Eshuriku, Obalufon, Orisha-oko, Shankpanna, Shango and Obatala among those most commonly worshipped; some of the divinities are borrowed from other tribes, and each deity has its day in the five-day week.
summary.zh: 約魯巴眾神俗稱四百零一；約翰遜主教指正確之數當為六百，分作兩班——如巴巴拉奧所言：右列二百，左列四百。最受崇奉者有伊法、奧杜杜瓦、奧班塔與奧班拉、奧舜、奧貢、耶莫雅、痘神、奧巴魯豐、農神、尚戈與奧巴塔拉等；亦有自他族引入之神，五日一週，各有其日。

sensitivity.note: Yoruba pantheon arithmetic recorded 1906 by Bishop Johnson; the 200/400 division matches the older Bini 201-Ebami reckoning. Cross-ref: yoruba-eware-201-spirits.

passages.text: The number of Yoruba gods commonly reckoned is 401, but it is strictly more correct to say that the number is 600, arranged generally under two divisions, 200, as the babalawos would say, placed on the right-hand side, and 400 on the left-hand side. But the gods more commonly worshipped are Ifa, Oduduwa, Obanta and Obanla his wife, Oshun, Ogun, Yemaja, Eshuriku, Obalufon, Orisha-oko, and Shankpanna, Shango and Obatala.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Some of the Yoruba divinities have been borrowed from other tribes: Shango from the Niger territory; Eka-Ifa from the Akoko tribe; and Aje from the Egbin or Popo tribe. Yorubans, whose worship is a recurring festival at which a particular divinity is worshipped, have from this circumstance often denominated a day in every cycle of five days from the name of the deity to whose worship it is devoted — the day of Jakuta (Shango), the day of Obatala, the day of Ifa, when he sits on a throne like a king; the day of Abameta; and the day of Yemaja, which is the day of Oro as well, when both Yemaja and the spirits of deceased ancestors are worshipped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Opele, the Slave Oracle of Ifa
title.zh: 奧佩萊——伊法座下的奴僕神諭

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the diviner's bowl at Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費占卜師的占碗）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: Behind each of Ifa's sixteen representative palm-nuts stand sixteen subordinate divinities: 256 odu in all, each with 1,680 traditional stories — a corpus no babalawo has ever memorised whole. Opele, Ifa's constant attendant and slave, is the oracle of eight flat pieces strung in two rows of four: cheaper, easier, consulted every morning, but a servant's answer not always to be relied on.
summary.zh: 伊法十六枚聖果仁之後各立十六位小神，合二百五十六「奧杜」，每奧杜附一千六百八十則傳統故事——無人能全數背誦。奧佩萊是伊法的貼身侍從與奴僕神諭：八片扁平木牌分兩排各四，占之較易，晨晨必占；然其應答僅是僕人代主之言，未必句句可恃。

sensitivity.note: Living Ifa practice (UNESCO-listed 2008); recorded 1906 by Bishop Johnson. The 'Owe ni Ifa npa' — Ifa speaks in parables — saying anchors the oracular hermeneutic.

passages.text: The great Oracle of the Yoruba country is Ifa, represented chiefly by sixteen palm nuts, each having from four to ten or more eyelets. Behind each one of these representative nuts are sixteen subordinate divinities; each one of the whole lot is termed an Odu, which means a chief, a head — altogether 256. Besides these there are sixteen other odus connected with each of the 256. There is a series of traditional stories, each of which is called a road, a pathway, or a course, and is connected with some particular odu; each odu is supposed to have 1,680 of these stories connected with it, and these, together with those of the other odus, every one aspiring to the office of babalawo is expected to commit to memory, though scarcely has anyone been found to perform the feat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Opele, or Opepere, is an oracle of inferior rank to Ifa, and is regarded as his constant attendant, commonly spoken of as his slave. He is always represented by eight flat pieces of wood, or metal, strung together in two rows of four; the disposition of one or other of these pieces when the whole ensign is thrown out upon the ground would represent a particular odu; and one of Opele's chief duties is to show to the babalawo what particular odu he should consult. Opele is often consulted because it carries less labour than consulting the master Ifa himself, but on matters of minor importance; its response would be that of a servant for his master, and is not always absolutely relied upon. Opele is expected to be consulted every morning; whilst a babalawo is expected to consult his Ifa every fifth day, the close of a week of oses or worshipping days. Hence the parable: "There is never a morning when a babalawo does not consult his Opele, as there is never a morning that a blacksmith is not called upon to sharpen a cutlass for a farmer."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Ela Has Descended: We Shall Die No More
title.zh: 埃拉已降世——吾儕不再死

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the yam fields where the Ela songs are sung, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊唱埃拉之歌的薯田）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: Ela is Ifa's great name of salvation: the strong and mighty Deliverer unconquerable by Death itself, the offspring of the hard stone from the bed of a spring. His devotees identify with that stone — "we are ourselves become Oyigiyigi, and will no longer die" — and cry "Ela has descended to the earth, we shall die no more; and this is Ifa's name." At yam harvest they split the Ela yam and sing Ela's festival song: our friend of the past year has come again.
summary.zh: 「埃拉」是伊法的救贖尊名：剛強無匹的拯救者，連死亡也不能勝過——他是泉底磐石所生。信眾以此石自比：「吾儕已成奧伊吉伊吉之石，不再死亡！」並高呼：「埃拉已降世，吾儕不再死——此即伊法之名。」收穫季節，信眾剖開「埃拉之薯」，唱起節歌：「埃拉重現了！去歲故人今又來，赴此一年一度的祭典。」

sensitivity.note: Living Ifa/Orunmila devotion recorded 1906; the Ela-saviour theology is a distinctive Yoruba soteriology. Presented as archival record of hymnody and rite.

passages.text: Ela is one of the many attributive names by which Ifa is described, and a very principal one: a contraction of the term Orunmila, intended to represent the divinity to all its worshippers principally as a Saviour and Deliverer, one that is strong and mighty and unconquerable by Death itself, so that all who look to him for help in trouble and against any other evil, death not excluded, will find their confidence has not been misplaced.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: He is sometimes described in songs of praises as Ela Osin, Ela the child of Osin the Ruler; sometimes as Ela omo Oyigi Ota-omi, Ela the offspring of a stone, the hard stone from the bed of a spring of water, an emblem of great strength; a quality which, believed in, enables devotees to identify themselves with him and regard themselves as free from death, saying, "Awa di oyigiyigi, a ki o ku" — we are ourselves become Oyigiyigi, the stone which gave birth to Ela, and will no longer die — or at other times to say, "Ela ti a ki o ku mo; Okiribiti, Ela ni oruko Ifa" — Ela has descended to the earth, we shall die no more, and this is Ifa's name.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: It is the divinity to which harvest offerings are always presented by worshippers, especially in the yam season before any portion of the harvest is partaken of, and when they are said to split the Ela yam — and when Orunmila is said to come and partake of the yam with them — singing lustily to Ela's praises: "Ela poko! Our friend of the past year has come again to observe the yearly festival; the anniversary has returned. I am come, O Iroko, lord of the cultivated field, to observe the yearly festival. O thou our worthy Father! the Son who hast descended from heaven to this earth, who hast placed us in the world."
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Orun Apaadi: The Heaven of Potsherds

region.en: The Yoruba upper world (symbolic pin: the sky-land above Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴上天之境（象徵定位：伊費上空的天界）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: The spirits of all the dead go after death to Orun, the heavens or world above, divided in two. One part is the heaven of sweet air and peace where the souls of the good are admitted; the other is Orun Apaadi, the world of potsherds, where the spirits of the wicked live after death as a heap of refuse, a mass of God-rejected souls, treated as potsherds flung to a dunghill — or as dry leaves covering an ear of corn, thrown into the fire. The soul is not liable to death, and the good return to be born again — hence the names Babatunde, our father has returned, and Iyabode, our mother has returned.
summary.zh: 人死之後，眾靈皆往「奧倫」——上天之界。天界分兩部：一為「甜風安寧之天」，善者之魂居之；一為「奧倫阿帕迪」——碎陶之界，惡者之靈如垃圾成堆、為神所棄，像擲向糞堆的破陶片，又如覆在穀穗上的枯葉，終歸火中。靈魂本無死；善靈重返人間再世——故名「巴巴通德」（父親歸來）、「伊亞博德」（母親歸來）。

sensitivity.note: Yoruba eschatology recorded 1906 by Bishop Johnson; reincarnation-within-lineage (Yiyi, the shooting forth of a branch) is a living Yoruba belief. The 'judgment after death' appears only in proverbial sayings.

passages.text: It teaches that the soul of man is not liable to death, and that after the death of the body, which results from its quitting it, it hovers about the earth for some time, and after this departs into the world of spirits above. The spirits of all the dead go after death to Orun, the heavens or the world above. It is divided into two parts. One part is commonly called Isalu Orun, or Orun Afejefere, the heaven of sweet air, or Orun Alafia, the heaven of peace and happiness, where the souls of all the good from this world are admitted and live after death; and another part is called Orun Apaadi, the world of potsherds, where the spirits of the wicked here pass to and live in after death as a heap of refuse and rubbish, a mass of God-rejected souls — treated there as potsherds are here, commonly flung to a dunghill.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sometimes this world is described as Orun Ihaririha, the heaven where both the sun and fire meet together, and where the roar of their united flames and heat is like the shout of a great multitude. The spirit of a good dead returns from the spirit world to be again born into this world, into the family of which it had before death been a visible part; hence, when a name would be given to a child, a babalawo is consulted to know whether the departed one who has returned has come through the father's or the mother's line — this accounts for names such as Babatunde, our father has returned, and Iyabode, our mother has returned. This transmigration is spoken of as Yiyi, the shooting forth of a branch.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Agberu, Who Carries the Sacrifices to Heaven

region.en: Yoruba country (symbolic pin: the heaven-ward path above the shrine, near Ile-Ife)
region.zh: 約魯巴地方（象徵定位：伊費近郊祠壇上空的天路）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: Sacrifices offered to the orishas, who stand as subordinate deities and mediators, are believed to be taken to the Great One by a spirit called Agberu, the carrier — Agberu who carries people's sacrifices to heaven. The basket in which he carries them is lined with Ifa's sacred leaves, each leaf a spoken wish: the toto leaf, that the offerer may be equal to those above him; the eyinriju leaf, that he may surpass others; the igberese leaf that accompanies a sacrifice to heaven; and the yeye leaf that brings blessing into our houses.
summary.zh: 獻給奧里莎（居於次神與中保之位）的祭品，相傳由一位名為「阿格貝魯」的神靈送呈至至尊——「阿格貝魯，捎祭上天者」。其背籃以伊法聖葉襯底，葉葉皆是祝詞：多多之葉，盼與上位者比肩；埃因里朱之葉，盼超越他人；伊格貝雷塞之葉，伴祭品同登天界；耶耶之葉，為家中帶來福澤。

sensitivity.note: Living sacrificial theology recorded 1906; the leaf-wish code is part of Ifa-associated practice.

passages.text: These sacrifices which are offered by heathens to their orishas, who occupy the place both of subordinate deities and mediators, are believed to be taken to the Great One by a spirit whom they denominate Agberu, the carrier, whose special business it is to take them to him and wait upon him with them. He goes by the title Agberu ti igbe ebo re orun — Agberu who carries people's sacrifices to heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: The basket in which he is supposed to carry the sacrifices to heaven is lined with leaves sacred to Ifa: the toto leaf, symbolical of the wish and prayer of the offerer that he may be equal to those who are before and above him; the eyinriju leaf, symbolical of his wish that he may surpass others; the Igberese leaf, generally described as the leaf which accompanies a sacrifice to heaven; and the Yeye leaf, often described as the yeye leaf that brings blessing into our houses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Oluwo Who Carried the Town's Sins

region.en: Yoruba royal city (symbolic pin: the Igbodu grove's three partitions, near Oyo)
region.zh: 約魯巴王城（象徵定位：奧約附近伊格博杜聖林三重門）

texts.period: Yoruba oral tradition; recorded 1906 (Johnson, in Dennett)

source.work: Bishop James Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in R. E. Dennett, At the Back of the Black Man's Mind (1906), Appendix

summary.en: The human victim chosen for the king's great sacrifice, called an Oluwo, is well fed while confined; then led through the streets — ashes thrown over his head, face painted with chalk — while people rush out to lay hands on him, transferring their sin, guilt, trouble and death to him. Through the Igbodu's three partitions he goes, sings his last song, and the announcement of his last word or groan is the signal for joy, drumming and dancing: the sacrifice is accepted, the divine wrath appeased.
summary.zh: 為王舉行大祭所選的人牲稱「奧魯沃」，圈禁期間養尊處優。祭日他沿街遊行——灰撒其首、白堊塗面——家家戶戶衝出門來撫摸其身，將自己一家老小的罪咎、災禍與死亡盡數轉嫁其身。隨後經伊格博杜聖林三重門而入，唱起訣別之歌；歌聲或呻吟一斷，全城便鑼鼓齊鳴、歌舞相慶——祭已受納，神怒平息。

sensitivity.note: Historical record of pre-colonial royal human sacrifice as described in 1906 by an African bishop of Yoruba origin; violence is described non-graphically. This is archival ethnography of a practice that colonial-era abolition ended — not a description of living Yoruba religion.

passages.text: The human victim chosen for sacrifice, who may be either a free-born or a slave, a person of noble or wealthy parentage or one of humble birth, is, after he has been chosen and marked out for the purpose, called an Oluwo. He is always well fed and nourished and supplied with whatever he should desire during the period of his confinement. When the occasion arrives for him to be sacrificed, he is commonly led about and paraded through the streets of the town or city of the sovereign who would sacrifice him for the well-being of his government and of every family and individual under it, in order that he might carry off the sin, guilt, misfortune and death of all without exception; ashes and chalk would be employed to hide his identity, the one being freely thrown over his head and his face painted with the latter, whilst individuals would often rush out of their houses to lay their hands upon him, that they might thus transfer to him their sin, guilt, trouble and death.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim. Historical ethnography of pre-colonial royal sacrifice; presented as record, not practice.

passages.text: This parading done, he is taken through a temporary sacred shed of palm and other tree branches — the Igbodu — and to its first division, where many persons might follow him, and through a second, where only the chiefs and other very important persons might escort and accompany him, and to a third, where only the babalawo and his official assistant, the Ajigbona, are permitted to enter with him. Here, after he himself has given out or started his last song, which is to be taken up by the large assembly of people who will have been waiting to hear his last word or his last groan, his head is taken off and his blood offered to the gods. The announcement of his last word or his last groan, heard and taken up by the people, would be a signal for joy, gladness and thanksgiving, and for drum-beating and dancing, as an expression of their gratification because their sacrifice has been accepted, the divine wrath is appeased, and the prospect of prosperity assured.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Johnson, Yoruba Heathenism, in Dennett (1906); not verbatim. Historical ethnography; presented as record, not practice.
